strengths: The paper introduces two novel and well-motivated compositional HJ-RL problems (RAA and RR) that meaningfully extend prior reach/avoid/reach-avoid formulations to dual-objective satisfaction, addressing a real gap between simple HJ-RL and full temporal-logic-based approaches.

Strong theoretical contribution: the authors rigorously prove (Theorems 1-3, with detailed appendix proofs spanning many pages) that RAA and RR values can be exactly decomposed into combinations of previously known avoid/reach/reach-avoid value functions, and prove necessity and sufficiency of state augmentation via a clean non-Markovian counterexample (Figure 3).

The paper carefully distinguishes its Bellman-value decomposition from superficially similar temporal-logic predicate algebra decompositions, with explicit counterexamples (Appendix L) showing why naive TL-style decomposition fails for value functions -- this is a nice piece of conceptual clarity.

DOHJ-PPO is a well-motivated practical algorithm with a stochastic relaxation (SRABE) justified theoretically (Theorem 4) and via policy-gradient derivation, and the coupled-reset design choice is empirically justified/ablated.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 4 diverse continuous-control environments (Hopper, F16, SafetyGym, HalfCheetah) with both RAA and RR tasks, compared against 10 baselines spanning Lagrangian, HJ-RL, STL/LTL-inspired, and MORL approaches, plus a DQN grid-world illustrative demo and a stochastic-dynamics robustness ablation.
Good related-work coverage situating the contribution relative to CMDPs, GCRL, LTL-RL, and HJ methods.
weaknesses: The main text is extremely dense and relies heavily on deferred appendix proofs; while thorough, the core theoretical exposition (Section 6) could better convey proof intuition in the main body, limiting accessibility.

DOHJ-PPO requires multiple additional actor and critic networks for decomposed objectives (Avoid/Reach-Avoid or two Reach subproblems plus composed networks), and the paper does not report additional compute/sample cost overhead relative to baselines, which matters for a claimed "little to no tuning" practical benefit.

Some CPPO baseline variants (e.g., CPPO-v1 in Appendix G) are acknowledged by the authors to perform very poorly, and the choice of which CPPO variant to report as "the" CPPO baseline in the main figures is not entirely clear, raising some concern about baseline framing.

The stochastic extension (SRABE) is only heuristically justified (interchanging extrema/expectation, acknowledged as an approximation without full guarantees), and the stochastic dynamics ablation is limited to a single environment (HalfCheetah) with only three seeds, limiting generality of the noise-robustness claims.

The generalization of decomposition principles beyond RAA/RR (e.g., to general nested temporal-logic-like specifications) is left entirely as future work, so the practical scope of the method remains restricted to these two specific compositions.

strengths: Provides a rigorous theoretical extension of the HJ-RL reachability framework (Fisac et al., Hsu et al., So et al.) to two novel and practically motivated dual-objective problems, Reach-Always-Avoid and Reach-Reach, with full proofs of decomposition (Theorems 1-2), state-augmentation necessity (Fig. 2, Theorem 3), and optimality of the augmented formulation.

The decomposition results are non-trivial and elegant: reducing RAA to an avoid problem plus a modified reach-avoid problem, and RR to two reach problems plus a modified reach problem, allowing reuse of existing tractable Bellman machinery rather than requiring new solvers or heavy reward engineering as in CMDP/Lagrangian or LTL/automaton-based approaches.

The derivation is carried through to a concrete, implementable algorithm (DO-HJ-PPO) via a Stochastic Reach-Avoid Bellman Equation and policy gradient result (Proposition 1), showing the theory is not purely abstract.

Empirical validation spans a qualitative DDQN grid-world (illustrating conceptual differences from plain reach/avoid values) and quantitative continuous-control tasks (Hopper, F16) against multiple reasonably designed baselines (CPPO variants, DSTL), with consistent improvements in success rate and steps-to-success.

Good, focused positioning relative to CMDP, multi-objective RL, goal-conditioned RL, and temporal logic RL, clarifying what advantage the explicit Bellman decomposition offers over surrogate/automaton-based approaches.
weaknesses: Empirical evaluation is fairly narrow: only two continuous-control environments (Hopper, F16), no reported variance/seeds or statistical significance for the 1,000-trajectory evaluations, and no ablation study results shown for design choices explicitly claimed to matter (e.g., 'coupled resets', which the text says are critical but for which no comparison numbers are given).

The CPPO baselines (v1-v3) are custom formulations designed by the authors themselves for this comparison, which raises some concern about baseline strength/fairness; the paper itself notes CPPOv1/v2 achieve 0% success in RR, suggesting the comparison may be somewhat one-sided.

The theory assumes deterministic dynamics; the extension to the stochastic PPO setting (SRABE) is presented with much less rigor (no convergence guarantee, just an adaptation of a prior stochastic Bellman heuristic), so the gap between the clean theoretical results and the practical algorithm is not fully closed.
Scalability of the framework beyond two objectives (more than one reward/penalty pair) is not discussed, limiting understanding of the method's generality.

The main text is extremely dense/terse (reads as a compressed conference brief with proofs entirely deferred to a long supplement), which hurts self-contained readability and makes it hard to verify key claims without consulting ~15 pages of appendix proofs.

No mention of code/data release for reproducibility, and experimental details (network sizes, exact reward scaling, environment resets) are only in the supplement, making independent reproduction harder.

Related work discussion in the main text is condensed to a single paragraph, which limits contextualization of how this method compares empirically or theoretically to other safety-liveness or multi-objective reachability methods beyond the chosen baselines.
